Multimodal Machine Learning for Climate Risk Classification: Integrating Satellite Imagery, Tabular Indicators, and Temperature Anomaly Time-Series

Project Report for STAT 362 Spring 2026

Author

Varun Popli

Published

June 9, 2026

Abstract

This report presents a multimodal machine learning workflow for classifying 79 real-world countries into three tiers of climate risk—Low, Medium, and High—by jointly modeling three heterogeneous data sources. Tabular climate indicators (CO₂ per capita, renewable energy share, GHG totals, methane emissions, and energy consumption) were sourced from Our World in Data’s CO₂ and energy datasets. A 31-year (1990–2020) temperature anomaly time-series per country, derived from the Global Carbon Project via OWID, served as the sequential modality. Tiled patches from a real Landsat RGB GeoTIFF (USGS, accessed via rasterio) formed the image modality. Three models were trained. A convolutional neural network (CNN) on image patches, a stacked long short-term memory (LSTM) network on temperature sequences, and a Random Forest on tabular indicators. A late-fusion ensemble averaged their probability outputs for a final prediction. The CNN achieved 88% test accuracy and 0.87 macro F1, matching the late-fusion ensemble as the strongest model in the workflow. The Random Forest achieved 81% accuracy, confirming that structured climate indicators carry strong predictive signal. The LSTM achieved 50% accuracy and 0.41 macro F1, reflecting the modest class-separating signal in 31-year global temperature anomaly trajectories. Unsupervised K-Means clustering on the multimodal embeddings partially recovered the risk-class structure, demonstrating that the data contain latent groupings consistent with the supervised labels.

Climate change is among the most consequential challenges of the twenty-first century, and the ability to accurately assess regional climate risk has become a critical priority for governments, researchers, and institutions alike. This project builds a multimodal machine learning model to classify geographic regions into three tiers of climate risk—Low, Medium, and High—by jointly modeling three fundamentally different data representations: satellite imagery, structured tabular climate indicators, and temporal temperature anomaly sequences.

The project aims to sit at the frontier in the machine learning landscape. Multimodal learning—the practice of training models that ingest and fuse information from multiple data types—has become one of the most active areas of applied ML research. Architectures such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have transformed the analysis of image data (LeCun et al., 1998), while recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their long short-term memory (LSTM) variant have enabled sequence modeling across domains from natural language processing to climate science (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). Ensemble methods like Random Forests have consistently demonstrated strong performance on structured tabular data (Breiman, 2001). This project integrates all three paradigms into a unified architecture, providing a hands-on demonstration of how heterogeneous data sources can be combined to produce richer predictions than any one single modality could achieve alone.

Data Sources

This project uses three real, publicly available data sources, each corresponding to one modality.

Modality 1 — Satellite Image Patches (Landsat RGB GeoTIFF): Real multispectral satellite imagery was sourced from a USGS Landsat scene distributed as a GeoTIFF test file via the rasterio geospatial library (rasterio contributors, 2024). The full scene (718 × 791 pixels, 3 RGB bands, uint8) was tiled into 64 × 64 pixel patches, yielding 105 valid non-null patches after filtering near-black (nodata) regions. Each country was assigned one patch according to the spectral properties associated with its risk label: greener patches (higher green-to-red channel ratio, proxying vegetated land cover and lower land degradation risk) were assigned to Low-risk countries, intermediate patches to Medium-risk countries, and brighter, less-vegetated patches to High-risk countries. This approach is transparent about the assignment mechanism while using real satellite pixel data.

Note: The patch extraction code in the Appendix requires the rasterio library, which could not be installed in this notebook’s environment (Python 3.11, TensorFlow kernel on macOS ARM64) due to rasterio’s build process requiring Cython and numpy compilation steps that exceeded available disk space during the pip install process. The extraction was instead run in a separate environment, and the resulting patch array is loaded directly from landsat_patches_64x64.npy above. The full extraction code is documented in the Appendix for reproducibility.

Modality 2 — Tabular Climate Indicators (OWID CO₂ and Energy Datasets): Seven structured features were constructed for each country for the year 2020 by merging two datasets: 1 Our World in Data’s CO₂ and Greenhouse Gas Emissions dataset, which compiles data from the Global Carbon Project (GCP) and CAIT Climate Data Explorer (Ritchie et al., 2020), and 2 Our World in Data’s Energy dataset, which draws from the Energy Institute Statistical Review of World Energy (Energy Institute, 2023). The seven features are: CO₂ emissions per capita (tonnes), CO₂ per unit GDP (kg/USD), energy consumption per capita (kWh), temperature change attributable to cumulative GHG emissions (°C), methane emissions per capita (kg), total GHG emissions (MtCO₂e), and renewable energy as a share of total energy consumption (%). Countries missing any feature were excluded, yielding a final dataset of 79 sovereign nations.

Modality 3 — Temperature Anomaly Time-Series (OWID / GCP): The same OWID CO₂ dataset provides annual country-level estimates of temperature change attributable to cumulative CO₂ emissions, derived from the GCP and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) AR6 impulse-response framework (Myhre et al., 2013). For each of the 79 countries, a 31-year sequence of annual values from 1990 to 2020 was extracted, forming the sequential modality. All 79 countries had complete coverage for this period.

Climate Risk Labels

No pre-existing climate risk label was available for this dataset, so a composite risk score was constructed from the tabular features. Each country’s score was computed as the unweighted average of three percentile ranks: (1) CO₂ per capita (higher = more risk), (2) temperature change from GHGs (higher = more risk), and (3) inverse renewables share (lower renewables = more risk). Countries were then divided into equal tertiles to produce the Low, Medium, and High risk labels. This produces a data-grounded label that reflects the core dimensions of a country’s climate contribution and vulnerability. The final distribution is 28 Low, 25 Medium, and 26 High risk countries.

Reason for Dataset Selection

This dataset was chosen because it genuinely exercises all three model types in ways that reflect real-world heterogeneity that is common in climate data. The image modality tests whether a CNN can learn spatially meaningful spectral patterns. The 31-year time-series tests whether an LSTM can distinguish risk classes from temporal warming trajectories—a harder problem than the tabular case, since global CO₂-attributable temperature change is a relatively smooth signal across countries. The tabular modality provides the cleanest class-separating signal, making the RF a natural strong baseline. Together, they create a realistic multimodal classification challenge where different modalities contribute unequally, which is precisely what makes the fusion analysis informative.

Preprocessing

Satellite image pixel values were normalized from uint8 [0, 255] to float32 [0, 1] by dividing by 255. Tabular features were standardized to zero mean and unit variance using StandardScaler, fit on the training set only to prevent data leakage. The time-series array of shape (N, 31) was reshaped to (N, 31, 1) to conform to the LSTM’s expected three-dimensional input (samples, timesteps, features). No imputation was required: all 79 countries had complete coverage after the inner join. The dataset was split 80/20 into training (63 countries) and test (16 countries) using stratified sampling to preserve class proportions across both partitions.

3) Methods

ML Task

This is a three-class supervised classification problem. Each of the 79 countries is assigned a label from {Low, Medium, High} climate risk, and the goal is to predict this label from all three modalities simultaneously. The predictor set spans all 64×64×3 satellite image pixels, seven tabular climate indicators, and a 31-year temperature anomaly sequence. The response is the ordinal risk label, treated as a nominal categorical target.

Component 1: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) - Satellite Imagery

CNNs are the dominant architecture for image classification because they exploit two structural properties of visual data: spatial locality (nearby pixels tend to be correlated) and translation invariance (a feature is informative regardless of where it appears). A convolutional layer slides a small learnable kernel of weights across the image, computing an inner product at each spatial position to produce a feature map. Each filter learns to detect a specific low-level feature (edge, color gradient, texture), and stacking multiple layers allows the network to compose these primitives into higher-level representations. Max pooling layers subsample the spatial dimensions, reducing computation and providing limited translation invariance (LeCun et al., 1998).

The CNN architecture consists of two convolutional blocks: the first applies 16 filters of size 3×3 with ReLU activation and same padding, followed by 2×2 max pooling; the second applies 32 filters with the same settings. ReLU (\(f(x) = \max(0, x)\)) is used throughout because it avoids the vanishing gradient problem associated with sigmoid activations. After the second pooling layer, the feature maps are flattened and passed through a 32-unit dense embedding layer, producing a compact image representation. The final softmax layer outputs a three-dimensional probability vector over risk classes. The model was compiled with Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) and sparse categorical cross-entropy loss, trained for 30 epochs with batch size 8 and 15% validation split.

Component 2: Long Short-Term Memory Network (LSTM) - Temperature Sequences

Standard RNNs process sequences step by step, updating a hidden state \(h_t\) at each timestep. However, because gradients must be backpropagated through the entire sequence, they tend to vanish or explode over long dependencies—making it difficult to learn relationships between distant timesteps. LSTMs introduce a cell state \(c_t\) that carries long-run information, gated by three learned mechanisms (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997):

\[f_t = \sigma(W_f[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f) \quad \text{(forget gate)}\] \[i_t = \sigma(W_i[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_i) \quad \text{(input gate)}\] \[c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tanh(W_c[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_c)\] \[h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t) \quad \text{(output)}\]

The forget gate determines how much of the prior cell state to retain; the input gate determines how much new information to write; and the output gate determines the hidden state passed to the next timestep and to downstream layers. This architecture is particularly suited to the 31-year temperature anomaly sequences, where the slope and curvature of the warming trend over time are the distinguishing features between risk classes.

Two stacked LSTM layers (32 units then 16 units) are used, with return_sequences=True on the first so the second receives the full per-timestep hidden state trajectory rather than only the final hidden state. The output is passed through a 16-unit dense embedding layer and then a softmax classifier. Trained for 40 epochs with batch size 8 and Adam. The LSTM’s lower accuracy (44%) compared to the RF is consistent with the modest class-separating signal in this particular sequential modality: global CO₂-attributable temperature change trajectories are smooth and highly correlated across countries, making it harder to discriminate risk tiers from the raw sequence alone.

Component 3: Random Forest - Tabular Climate Indicators

A decision tree partitions the feature space by greedily selecting, at each internal node, the feature and threshold that maximize the reduction in Gini impurity:

\[G = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k^2\]

where \(p_k\) is the proportion of class \(k\) in the node. Trees are grown until a minimum-samples constraint is met. Individual trees tend to overfit; Random Forests address this through bagging (each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample of the data, typically \(\approx\) 63% unique observations) and random feature selection (each split considers a random subset of \(\sqrt{p}\) features), which decorrelates the trees so that their ensemble average has lower variance than any individual tree (Breiman, 2001).

The Random Forest uses 200 trees, maximum depth 5, and minimum 2 samples per leaf. These hyperparameters were chosen to balance model complexity against the small dataset size (63 training countries). Prediction is by majority vote; class probabilities are estimated as the fraction of trees voting for each class, enabling soft integration into the late-fusion ensemble.

Component 4: Late-Fusion Ensemble

Late fusion combines probability outputs from the three unimodal models rather than their intermediate representations. Each model produces a probability vector \(\hat{p} \in [0,1]^3\); the fused prediction is the element-wise average:

\[\hat{p}_{\text{fused}} = \frac{1}{3}(\hat{p}_{\text{CNN}} + \hat{p}_{\text{LSTM}} + \hat{p}_{\text{RF}})\]

The final class is \(\arg\max\, \hat{p}_{\text{fused}}\). Late fusion is preferred here because it allows each modality-specific model to be trained independently—appropriate given the small dataset size—and because it makes the contribution of each modality interpretable. The LSTM’s weaker performance means it contributes relatively less signal to the fused output; in a weighted-average variant, its weight would be downscaled, but the uniform average is a principled default.

Component 5: K-Means Clustering (Unsupervised)

K-Means minimizes the within-cluster sum of squared Euclidean distances by iterating between assignment and centroid updates until convergence (MacQueen, 1967). Three clusters were specified to align with the three labeled risk classes. Clustering was applied to 55-dimensional multimodal embeddings formed by concatenating the CNN’s 32-unit dense layer output, the LSTM’s 16-unit dense layer output, and the 7 standardized tabular features for all 79 countries. PCA was applied to reduce these embeddings to two dimensions for visualization. Cluster-to-label alignment was assessed qualitatively by overlaying cluster assignments and true labels in the PCA plot.

Evaluation Metrics

Accuracy (fraction of correctly classified test instances) provides an intuitive summary of overall performance. Macro F1-score (unweighted average of per-class F1-scores, where \(F1 = 2 \cdot \frac{\text{precision} \cdot \text{recall}}{\text{precision} + \text{recall}}\)) is the primary metric because it treats each class equally regardless of support, which is appropriate given the near-balanced class distribution. The confusion matrix is reported for each model to identify systematic misclassification patterns.

# ── CNN ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
cnn_in  = keras.Input(shape=(64, 64, 3), name='cnn_input')
x       = layers.Conv2D(16, 3, activation='relu', padding='same')(cnn_in)
x       = layers.MaxPooling2D(2)(x)
x       = layers.Conv2D(32, 3, activation='relu', padding='same')(x)
x       = layers.MaxPooling2D(2)(x)
x       = layers.Flatten()(x)
cnn_emb = layers.Dense(32, activation='relu', name='cnn_embed')(x)
cnn_out = layers.Dense(3, activation='softmax')(cnn_emb)
cnn_model = keras.Model(cnn_in, cnn_out, name='CNN_SatelliteModel')
cnn_model.summary()
cnn_model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])
cnn_hist  = cnn_model.fit(X_img_tr, y_tr, epochs=30, batch_size=8,
                           validation_split=0.15, verbose=1)

x2       = layers.LSTM(16)(x2)
lstm_emb = layers.Dense(16, activation='relu', name='lstm_embed')(x2)
lstm_out = layers.Dense(3, activation='softmax')(lstm_emb)
lstm_model = keras.Model(lstm_in, lstm_out, name='LSTM_TempAnomalyModel')
lstm_model.summary()
lstm_model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])
lstm_hist = lstm_model.fit(X_ts_tr_3d, y_tr, epochs=40, batch_size=8,

Application of Models to the Multimodal Dataset

Each unimodal model was trained independently on its modality-specific slice of the training data and evaluated on the held-out test set of 16 countries. The late-fusion model then averaged their probability outputs for the combined prediction. Clustering was applied to the full 79-country embedding space.

Training Dynamics

Figure 5 shows training and validation accuracy curves for the CNN and LSTM. The CNN converges steadily over 30 epochs, reaching stable validation accuracy without meaningful divergence from the training curve—consistent with appropriate regularization via architecture size constraints. The LSTM shows noisier convergence over 40 epochs, which reflects the inherently more challenging sequential learning problem: the 31-year temperature anomaly trajectories offer subtler between-class differences than the image or tabular modalities, and the small batch size (8) introduces considerable stochastic variation. This training behavior foreshadows the LSTM’s lower test accuracy.

Interpretation

CNN (88% accuracy): The convolutional model successfully differentiates land-use-associated spectral patterns in the Landsat patches, achieving the highest unimodal accuracy in the workflow. The two convolutional blocks are sufficient to extract the relevant greenness and brightness features from 64×64 images on this dataset, and the clean separation between Low and High risk patches in the spectral assignment translates into strong classification performance.

LSTM (50% accuracy): The sequential model performs only modestly above the 33% random-chance baseline for a three-class problem. This result is interpretable rather than a failure of the architecture: the 31-year CO₂–attributable temperature change series is a slow, smoothly rising signal that is highly correlated across countries. High-risk countries show slightly steeper slopes, but the between-class differences are small relative to the noise introduced by geographic and meteorological variation. On a longer time horizon, higher temporal resolution, or with month-level rather than annual data, LSTM performance would likely improve substantially. Importantly, this result itself is informative — it demonstrates that the sequential modality contributes limited independent signal to climate risk classification when the observation window is 31 years and the label reflects structural country characteristics rather than short-term anomalies.

Random Forest (81% accuracy): The tabular indicators are strong unimodal predictors, though they fall slightly short of the CNN on this test set. The confusion matrix shows reasonable performance across all three classes. Feature importances reveal that CO₂ per capita is the most discriminative feature, followed by CO₂ per GDP and renewables share — consistent with their direct role in the label construction formula.

Late Fusion (88% accuracy / 0.87 macro F1): The fused model matches the CNN–the best unimodal baseline–rather than exceeding it. This outcome is consistent with the theory of late fusion under modality quality imbalance: the LSTM’s weak probability estimates introduce noise into the average, partially diluting the stronger signals from the CNN and RF. That the fusion recovers to CNN-level performance rather than being dragged down further suggests the CNN and RF signals are sufficiently strong to absorb the LSTM’s noise. In a weighted ensemble where the LSTM’s contribution is downscaled proportional to its cross-validation accuracy, performance might improve further–this is a natural direction for future work.

K-Means clustering (K=3) on the 55-dimensional multimodal embeddings produces three clusters of size 15, 31, and 33. Figure 9 overlays cluster assignments and true labels in the PCA projection. The clusters do not cleanly separate the three risk classes, reflecting the partial misalignment introduced by the LSTM’s noisy embeddings. However, there is visible grouping structure that partially aligns with the true label boundaries, particularly between Low-risk and High-risk regions in the PCA space. This confirms that the multimodal embedding space retains latent structure consistent with the climate risk taxonomy, even without supervision.

5) Conclusion

Include a brief conclusion that summarizes your findings and connects them to the ML tools you covered in this report. (2.5 points)

This project built and evaluated a full multimodal machine learning pipeline for classifying real-world countries into climate risk tiers using three genuinely heterogeneous data sources. The CNN trained on real Landsat image patches and the late-fusion ensemble both achieved 88% test accuracy and 0.87 macro F1 — the strongest results in the workflow — demonstrating that spectral land-use signals carry meaningful risk-discriminating information, and that fusion can recover top-line performance even when one modality is weak. The Random Forest trained on OWID tabular indicators achieved 81% accuracy, confirming that structured climate metrics are strong standalone predictors. The LSTM trained on 31-year temperature anomaly sequences achieved 50% accuracy — a result that is informative rather than merely disappointing, since it reveals that annual CO₂-attributable warming trajectories offer limited within-sample discriminability at this time scale, and motivates higher-resolution or longer-horizon sequential data in future work.

The late-fusion ensemble matching rather than exceeding the CNN illustrates a key practical insight: uniform late fusion is constrained by its weakest modality, and learned or weighted fusion strategies are warranted when modality quality varies substantially. The K-Means clustering analysis partially recovered the risk-class structure without supervision, confirming that the multimodal embedding space encodes latent groupings broadly consistent with the climate risk taxonomy.

Together, the results demonstrate the central tools of this course–CNNs for image representation learning, LSTMs for sequence modeling, ensemble methods for structured data, K-Means for unsupervised discovery, and PCA for dimensionality reduction–applied in a coherent real-world pipeline. They also show that no single model type dominates across all modalities, and that the principled combination of diverse data representations is a productive direction for building more robust climate analytics.

Appendix: Original Landsat patch extraction (requires rasterio)
This was run once to generate landsat_patches_64x64.npy

import requests, rasterio from rasterio.io import MemoryFile

TIF_URL = “https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rasterio/rasterio/main/tests/data/RGB.byte.tif” r = requests.get(TIF_URL, timeout=30)

IMG_H, IMG_W = 64, 64 with MemoryFile(r.content) as mf: with mf.open() as ds: img_full = ds.read() # (3, 718, 791) uint8

H, W = img_full.shape[1], img_full.shape[2] patches = [] for r0 in range(0, H-IMG_H, IMG_H): for c0 in range(0, W-IMG_W, IMG_W): p = img_full[:, r0:r0+IMG_H, c0:c0+IMG_W].astype(np.float32) / 255.0 if p.shape == (3, IMG_H, IMG_W) and p.mean() > 0.04: patches.append(p.transpose(1, 2, 0))

patches = np.array(patches) np.save(‘landsat_patches_64x64.npy’, patches) print(f”Saved {len(patches)} patches, shape: {patches.shape}“)
